label: Destination MAC
explanation: The hardware address of the network interface this frame is being sent to. MAC addresses are 6 bytes and uniquely identify a device on a local network segment.

symbolicValues.FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF: Broadcast — sent to all devices on the local network

label: Source MAC
explanation: The hardware address of the network interface that sent this frame. Used by switches to learn which port a device is connected to.

label: EtherType
explanation: Identifies the protocol carried in the payload. Values above 0x0600 indicate a protocol type; values below indicate the payload length (IEEE 802.3).

label: Version
explanation: IP protocol version. Always 4 for IPv4 packets. The first nibble of the IP header.

label: IHL (Header Length)
explanation: Internet Header Length — the number of 32-bit words in the IP header. The minimum value is 5 (20 bytes). Values above 5 indicate options are present.

label: DSCP (Differentiated Services)
explanation: Differentiated Services Code Point — used by routers to prioritize traffic. Higher-priority traffic (e.g., VoIP) can be marked to receive preferential treatment.

symbolicValues.0: Best Effort — default, no special priority

label: Total Length
explanation: The total size of the IP packet in bytes, including the header and payload. The maximum value is 65,535 bytes.

label: TTL (Time to Live)
explanation: Decremented by 1 at each router hop. When it reaches 0, the packet is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent back. Prevents packets from looping forever.

symbolicValues.255: Maximum — typically set by network equipment

label: Protocol
explanation: Identifies the transport-layer protocol carried in the IP payload.

label: Source IP
explanation: The IPv4 address of the sender. Routers use this to know where to send replies.

symbolicValues.127.0.0.1: Loopback — traffic staying on the same machine

label: Destination IP
explanation: The IPv4 address of the intended recipient. Routers forward the packet toward this address.

symbolicValues.255.255.255.255: Limited broadcast — sent to all hosts on the local network

label: Source Port
explanation: The port number on the sender's side. Ephemeral (client) ports are typically in the range 49152–65535. Well-known ports (0–1023) are assigned to standard services.

label: Destination Port
explanation: The port number on the receiver's side. Identifies which application or service should receive this segment.

label: Sequence Number
explanation: Identifies the position of the first byte of this segment in the overall data stream. TCP uses sequence numbers to reassemble out-of-order segments and detect missing data.

label: Acknowledgment Number
explanation: When the ACK flag is set, this field contains the sequence number of the next byte the sender expects to receive. It confirms all bytes up to this number have been received.

label: Flags
explanation: Control bits that manage the state of the TCP connection. Multiple flags can be set simultaneously.

symbolicValues.SYN: Synchronize — initiates a connection (first step of three-way handshake)
symbolicValues.PSH: Push — tells the receiver to deliver data to the application immediately
symbolicValues.URG: Urgent — indicates urgent data is present

label: Window Size
explanation: The number of bytes the sender is willing to receive before requiring an acknowledgment. A larger window allows more data in flight and improves throughput on high-latency links.

label: Source Port
explanation: The port number on the sender's side. For UDP, this is optional — a value of 0 means the sender does not require a reply.

label: Destination Port
explanation: The port number of the target application. UDP delivers the datagram to this port without establishing a connection first.

label: Length
explanation: The total length of the UDP datagram in bytes, including the 8-byte header and the payload. The minimum value is 8 (header only, no payload).

label: Checksum
explanation: An error-detection value covering the UDP header and payload. A value of 0x0000 means the checksum was not computed (optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6).

label: Type
explanation: Identifies the category of ICMP message. Different types serve different diagnostic or control purposes.

symbolicValues.0: Echo Reply — response to a ping
symbolicValues.3: Destination Unreachable — packet could not be delivered
symbolicValues.11: Time Exceeded — TTL reached zero (used by traceroute)

label: Code
explanation: Provides additional detail within an ICMP type. For example, Type 3 (Destination Unreachable) has codes that specify whether the network, host, port, or protocol was unreachable.

label: Checksum
explanation: Error-detection value covering the entire ICMP message. The receiver recalculates this and discards the message if it does not match.

label: Transaction ID
explanation: A 16-bit identifier assigned by the client. The DNS server copies this value into its response so the client can match replies to outstanding queries.

label: Flags
explanation: A 16-bit field encoding the message type, opcode, and status. Key bits include QR (query/response), AA (authoritative answer), TC (truncated), RD (recursion desired), and RA (recursion available).

symbolicValues.QR=0: Query — the client is asking a question
symbolicValues.AA=1: Authoritative Answer — the server owns this zone
symbolicValues.TC=1: Truncated — response was too large for UDP, retry with TCP
symbolicValues.RD=1: Recursion Desired — client wants the server to resolve on its behalf
symbolicValues.RA=1: Recursion Available — the server supports recursive queries

label: Question Count
explanation: The number of questions in the Question section. Typically 1 — most DNS messages contain a single query.

label: Answer Count
explanation: The number of resource records in the Answer section. A value of 0 in a response means the name was not found (NXDOMAIN).

label: Query Name
explanation: The domain name being looked up, encoded as a sequence of length-prefixed labels (e.g., 'www.example.com' → 3www7example3com0).

label: Record Type
explanation: Specifies what kind of DNS record is being requested or returned.
